newsitem.title: CANADA: Funeral takeover war puts industry under microscope.
newsitem.headline: Funeral takeover war puts industry under microscope.

text.p: The $2.9 billion battle by North America's biggest funeral home chain to acquire its closest rival is drawing attention to accusations by consumer watchdogs that industry practices are unfair to consumers.

Vancouver-based Loewen Group Inc., the second-biggest owner of funeral homes and cemeteries in North America, last week spurned a sweetened $45-a-share offer from industry giant Service Corp. International of Houston.

Since the publication of Jessica Mitford's expose, "The American Way of Death" in 1962, the $15-billion-a-year U.S. funeral industry has been dogged by allegations it overcharges and exploits the bereaved.

Although the takeover battle is expected to last for months, consumer activists -- and, not surprisingly, Loewen itself -- are voicing concerns the deal could further reduce competition and allow prices to rise faster.

"The amalgamation of the two companies is going to create monopolies," said Lisa Carlson, executive director of the non-profit Funeral and Memorial Societies of America and a vocal critic of the funeral industry.
"It's heads-up time for consumers," she said. "I think both (companies) are bad in their tactics."
Neither Service, which owns 3,309 funeral homes, crematoria and cemeteries, nor Loewen, which has 1,189 properties, responded to requests for comment.

But as part of its defense, Loewen filed an anti-trust lawsuit against Service. It also said that six American states, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and the Canadian government were probing the "anti-competitive" impact of the takeover.
Service has said it does not foresee any anti-trust problems. It believes it can satisfy regulators by selling a limited number of properties when it combines the two companies' operations.
Loewen and Service have prospered by buying up small independent funeral homes and then increasing their profits by cutting costs and centralizing management.
But consumer watchdogs said prices at mortuaries owned by the two chains are higher than at independents and up to 75 percent higher than the national average funeral cost of about $4,456.
"Consumers so far are not sharing in the cost savings. That is going to the stockholder," said Lee Norrgard, manager of consumer affairs for the American Association of Retired Persons."
Indeed, some critics believe Service may seek to raise prices even further after a merger.
"Somebody is going to have to pay the billions (that Loewen) will cost and that's the consumer," said Lawrence Little, a partner in a Canadian company seeking to franchise low-cost funeral services.
"This bidding frenzy is drawing consumer attention to the entire industry ... and focusing the consumer on the high dollars (the chains) charge," he said
Investment analysts generally disagreed, saying Service would continue to face about the same amount of competition because there was little overlap between the two chains.
Moreover, they noted that most consumers do not shop for funeral services based on price.
"I don't think this would affect the consumer landscape at all," said Todd Richter, an analyst who follows the funeral industry for Dean Witter.
The U.S. funeral industry remains highly fragmented with about 85 percent of mortuaries owned by independent companies or families.
While Loewen is stronger in rural areas and Service concentrates on cities, their combined market share would amount be about 10 percent nationwide.

In certain markets, however, their combined market share is much higher. For example, the two companies have about 31 percent of the funeral homes in Hawaii, 24 percent in Florida and 24 percent in Nevada, said analyst Susan Little of brokerage Raymond James.
New York's Attorney General is already investigating Service and is certain to scrutinize the takeover, said spokesman Chris McKenna.
Service handles one in six funerals in the state and owns three-quarters of the Jewish funeral homes in Manhattan, he said.
"There are potential monopoly implications ... and those issues would accelerate if Loewen were assumed by Service," said McKenna.
